tip: L' is the elided article (il/la → l') before a vowel: l'uomo, l'amica. Gender is hidden by elision.
Italian usually drops subject pronouns: 'mangio la pasta' is more natural than 'io mangio'. Use 'io' only for emphasis or contrast.
Italian drops subject pronouns in casual speech – 'Mangio la pasta' is more natural than 'Io mangio la pasta'.
'Guardare' = to watch/look at. No preposition needed: 'guarda la televisione'. Regular -are verb.
'-Are' verbs with 'tu': cucinare → cucini. The -i ending is the same for all three verb types with 'tu'.
The 'noi' form always ends in -iamo: prepariamo, corriamo, partiamo. This is consistent across all verb types.
'Con + noun' forms adverbial phrases: 'con attenzione' (carefully), 'con calma' (calmly). Alternative to -mente adverbs.
Unlike English, Italian uses the definite article with languages: 'Parlo l'italiano' (I speak Italian).
'Abitare' = to live (somewhere). 'In centro' = downtown/in the center. 'In' without article before general areas.
This -ire verb adds -isc- before the ending (capisco, finisco, preferisco). This is common for many -ire verbs.
'Amare' = to love (stronger than 'piacere'). 'La musica' uses the article – Italian uses definite articles with abstract nouns.
'Giocare a' + sport: 'gioco a tennis'. Use 'a' before sports. 'Giocare' has a soft g before -o: 'gioco'.
Verb endings show who: mangio (I), mangi (you), mangia (he/she). Subject pronouns are for emphasis only, not the default.
Dire (to say) is irregular: dico, dici, dice, diciamo, dite, dicono. From Latin "dicere".
Italians drop subject pronouns: mangio la pasta already means "I eat pasta". io mangio adds emphasis. Skip io/tu unless contrasting.
'A' before cities: 'abitano a Roma'. Use 'in' before countries: 'in Italia'. The preposition depends on city vs. country.
Double negation is required in Italian: 'Non parlo mai' = I never speak (literally: not speak never).
-ire verb: 'aprire' (to open). Third person: apre.
In Italian, you 'take' a coffee (prendere un caffè) – you don't 'have' or 'drink' it in casual speech.
'In' before countries: 'vive in Italia'. Use 'a' before cities. No article needed with 'in' + country name.
Italian questions often just use rising intonation – no word order change needed: 'Parli italiano?' = Do you speak Italian?
'Ascoltare' = to listen to. The 'to' is built in: 'ascolta la musica'. No preposition needed.
Italian word order is flexible: 'Mangio la pizza' and 'La pizza la mangio' both work, with different emphasis.
'A casa' = at home / homeward. 'Tornare a casa' = to go back home. No article needed with 'casa' in this set phrase.
In Italian, the subject pronoun (io, tu, lui) is usually dropped – the verb ending tells you who's speaking.
'Ricevere' is a regular -ere verb: ricevo, ricevi, riceve. The -ere conjugation: -o, -i, -e, -iamo, -ete, -ono.
'Bisogna' + infinitive = one must/it's necessary to. Impersonal – no subject needed: 'Bisogna studiare'.
'Da' = from/since/at someone's place: 'Vado da Marco' = I'm going to Marco's. Very versatile preposition.
Reflexive verbs need a pronoun: `mi chiamo` (I call myself = my name is), `si lava` (he washes himself). The pronoun matches the subject – mi/ti/si/ci/vi/si.
-ire verb with -isc- pattern: 'pulire' (to clean) → pulisco, pulisci, pulisce.
In Italian, professions often skip the article: 'Sono medico' (I'm a doctor), not 'sono un medico'.
'Credere in' = to believe in. 'Credere a' = to believe someone. The preposition changes the meaning.
Adverbs of frequency (sempre, spesso, mai) go after the verb: 'Mangio sempre la pasta' = I always eat pasta.
-ire verb: seguire (to follow). Regular conjugation: seguo, segui, segue, seguiamo, seguite, seguono.
'Bello' follows a special pattern before nouns (like articles): bel ragazzo, bell'uomo, bei ragazzi.
Endings hint at gender: -o usually m, -a usually f. But la mano is f, il problema is m. The article is the real signal.
'Andare' (to go) and 'venire' (to come) are opposite – 'venire' implies coming toward the speaker.
'Bere' (to drink) is irregular: bevo, bevi, beve, beviamo, bevete, bevono. One of the most common irregular verbs.
Fare (to do/make) is irregular: faccio, fai, fa, facciamo, fate, fanno. From Latin "facere".
Sapere (to know facts) is irregular: so, sai, sa, sappiamo, sapete, sanno. Compare with conoscere (to know people/places).
Volere (to want) is irregular: voglio, vuoi, vuole, vogliamo, volete, vogliono. A modal verb.
Avere (to have) is irregular: ho, hai, ha, abbiamo, avete, hanno. Also used as an auxiliary in compound tenses.
`stare` for how you are right now: `come stai?` (how are you?), `sto bene` (I'm fine). With permanent traits switch to `essere`.
Yes/no questions in Italian mainly use rising intonation. Word order can stay the same, though subject-verb inversion is also possible for emphasis.
"Stare + gerundio" forms the Italian progressive: "sto parlando" (I am speaking right now).
'Arrivare' is regular -are but uses 'essere' in passato prossimo: 'è arrivato/a'. Here in present tense.
Reflexive isn't always literal in English: `ricordarsi` = to remember, `arrabbiarsi` = to get angry. If the dictionary form ends in -si, you need the matching pronoun.
'In' + indefinite article for workplaces: 'lavoro in un ristorante'. 'In' doesn't contract with indefinite articles.
Uscire (to go out) is irregular: esco, esci, esce, usciamo, uscite, escono. Note the "esc-" stem in some forms.
After expressions of wish/doubt/opinion + `che`, Italian uses subjunctive (congiuntivo). `Voglio che tu venga` (not vieni) = 'I want you to come'.
Essere (to be) is irregular: sono, sei, è, siamo, siete, sono. One of the most important Italian verbs.
Object pronouns sit before the verb: `lo vedo` (I see him/it), not `vedo lo`. Lo/la/li/le match gender and number of what they replace.

Modal verbs (dovere, potere, volere) attach directly to the infinitive: `devo studiare`, `posso aiutare`, `voglio mangiare`. No preposition needed – unlike English's clunkier 'have to' / 'be able to'.
'Camminare al parco' = to walk to the park. 'Al' = a+il (contraction). All -are 'noi' forms: -iamo.
'Leggere' = to read. Irregular -ere verb: leggo, leggi, legge, leggiamo, leggete, leggono. Double 'g' throughout.
'Mangiare' keeps the -i- before -a: 'mangia' (he eats). But drops it before -i: 'mangi' (you eat).
'Vivere' = to live. Regular -ere: vivo, vivi, vive. 'In periferia' = in the suburbs.
'Correre' = to run. Irregular past participle: 'corso'. 'Al parco' = to/at the park.
Andare (to go) is irregular: vado, vai, va, andiamo, andate, vanno. Note the "v" root in several forms.

english: They say it would rain tomorrow.
tip: Conditional used for reported/unconfirmed info.
